Judges 1.summary: After Joshua's death, Judah is chosen to lead fighting against remaining Canaanite groups and joins forces with Simeon. Judah defeats Adonibezek, and the chapter recounts fighting in Jerusalem, Hebron, Debir, and other places (Judges 1:1–20). Caleb promises his daughter Achsah in marriage to the conqueror of Debir; Othniel succeeds, and Achsah asks Caleb for springs to supplement her land (Judges 1:11–15). Yet victory is incomplete: Benjamin does not expel the Jebusites from Jerusalem, and several tribes leave Canaanite populations in place, sometimes subjecting them to forced labor rather than displacing them (Judges 1:21–36). Israel has the land on paper, but not in fact.
Judges 1.whereWeAre: Joshua ended with Joshua's death and Israel's promise to serve the LORD. Now the tribes keep fighting for their land, but tribe after tribe fails to drive out the Canaanites. Chapter 2 explains what that failure will cost.

keyFigures.name: Othniel

keyThemes.explanation: The tribes begin by asking the LORD who should go up first.
Tribe after tribe leaves the Canaanites in the land.
Achsah asks for springs because land without water is little use.

Judges 2.summary: The angel of the LORD confronts Israel at Bochim over failure to honor the covenant and the resulting danger of rival worship; the people weep and sacrifice (Judges 2:1–5). After a retrospective account of Joshua's death and the faithful elders, the narrative says a later generation did not know the LORD's works and began serving Baal and Ashtaroth (Judges 2:6–13). God allows oppressors to trouble Israel, yet raises judges who deliver them; after a judge dies, the people turn again to corrupt practices (Judges 2:14–19). This sets the pattern for the whole book: Israel sins, suffers, cries out, is rescued, and falls away again.
Judges 2.whereWeAre: Chapter 1 showed the tribes leaving Canaanites in the land. Here the angel of the LORD rebukes Israel, and a new generation arises "which knew not the LORD" (Judges 2:10). The chapter lays out the cycle of sin and rescue that runs through the book, starting with the first judges in chapter 3.

keyFigures.name: The angel of the LORD
keyFigures.role: Rebukes Israel at Bochim for making peace with the Canaanites.

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: Weep and offer sacrifices, then a later generation serves Baal.

keyFigures.name: The LORD

keyFigures.name: The judges

A new generation arises "which knew not the LORD, nor yet the works which he had done for Israel."
God lets enemies oppress Israel but keeps raising up judges to save them.

Judges 3.summary: The opening identifies nations left in the land and says Israel's interaction with them became a test of covenant loyalty; intermarriage and service to other gods follow (Judges 3:1–6). Under the rule of Chushanrishathaim, Othniel receives the Spirit of the LORD and delivers Israel (Judges 3:7–11). Later Moab's King Eglon, allied with Ammon and Amalek, subjugates Israel; Ehud delivers tribute, kills Eglon during a private audience, escapes, and rallies Israel to defeat Moabite forces (Judges 3:12–30). A brief final notice credits Shamgar with striking down six hundred Philistines using an oxgoad (Judges 3:31). Three very different men each deliver Israel.
Judges 3.whereWeAre: Chapter 2 laid out the pattern: Israel sins, an enemy oppresses them, they cry out, and God sends a judge. This chapter shows it three times, with Othniel, Ehud, and Shamgar. Chapter 4 brings the next crisis, a Canaanite king with iron chariots.

keyFigures.name: Othniel
keyFigures.role: Son of Kenaz and the first judge, who defeats Chushanrishathaim.

keyFigures.name: Chushanrishathaim
keyFigures.role: King of Mesopotamia, who rules Israel eight years.

keyFigures.name: Ehud

keyFigures.name: Eglon
keyFigures.role: King of Moab, who rules Israel eighteen years.

keyFigures.name: Shamgar
keyFigures.role: Kills six hundred Philistines with an ox goad.

keyThemes.explanation: The nations are left "to prove Israel" and see whether they will obey.
When Israel cries out, the LORD raises up Othniel to deliver them.
A left-handed man and a farmer with an ox goad both save Israel.

Judges 4.summary: After Ehud's death, Israel suffers under Jabin, a Canaanite king at Hazor, whose commander Sisera has nine hundred iron chariots (Judges 4:1–3). Deborah, a prophet and judge, summons Barak with a command to gather troops from Naphtali and Zebulun against Sisera. Barak agrees to go only if Deborah accompanies him; she foretells that the honor of Sisera's death will go to a woman (Judges 4:4–10). At Mount Tabor and near the Kishon, the LORD throws Sisera's army into confusion, and Barak pursues it (Judges 4:11–16). Sisera flees into Jael's tent, where Jael kills him; Israel grows stronger against Jabin (Judges 4:17–24).
Judges 4.whereWeAre: After Ehud's rescue in chapter 3, Israel sins again and falls under Jabin and his captain Sisera. Deborah sends Barak to fight, and Sisera dies at the hand of a woman, Jael. Chapter 5 is the song Deborah and Barak sing about the victory.

keyFigures.name: Barak

keyFigures.name: Sisera

keyFigures.name: Jael

keyFigures.name: Jabin
keyFigures.role: King of Canaan, who rules from Hazor.

keyFigures.name: The LORD

keyThemes.explanation: Deborah, a prophetess, tells Barak what God has commanded.
"the LORD discomfited Sisera, and all his chariots."
As Deborah said, "the LORD shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman."

Judges 5.summary: Deborah and Barak sing a victory poem celebrating the LORD's intervention and honoring those who volunteered (Judges 5:1–11). The song summons memories of divine appearances, praises participants from tribes such as Ephraim, Benjamin, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and rebukes groups that stayed away (Judges 5:12–18). It describes kings fighting by the waters of Megiddo, the torrent Kishon sweeping enemies away, and a curse on Meroz for not helping (Judges 5:19–23). Jael is celebrated, while the song poignantly imagines Sisera's mother awaiting his return (Judges 5:24–30). It ends by wishing the LORD's enemies destroyed and his lovers strong; the land then has rest for forty years (Judges 5:31).
Judges 5.whereWeAre: Sisera was defeated in chapter 4. Now Deborah and Barak sing about the battle, praising the tribes that came and shaming those that stayed home. After forty years of rest, chapter 6 brings a new enemy, Midian.

keyFigures.name: The tribes who came
keyFigures.role: Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir, Zebulun, Issachar, and Naphtali, praised for fighting.

keyFigures.name: The tribes who stayed home

keyThemes.explanation: Deborah and Barak lead the people in praising God for the victory.
Some tribes come to fight, and others stay with their flocks.
"The stars in their courses fought against Sisera," and the river Kishon sweeps the enemy away.
Jael's victory is set against Sisera's mother waiting for a son who will not return.

Judges 6.summary: Midianite oppression drives Israelites to hide crops and shelter in mountain strongholds; a prophet first confronts their disobedience (Judges 6:1–10). The angel of the LORD appears to Gideon as he threshes wheat in a winepress. Gideon questions Israel's circumstances and receives a commission and sign (Judges 6:11–24). At night he tears down his father's altar to Baal, cuts down the Asherah, and builds an altar to the LORD; the townspeople threaten him, but Joash challenges Baal to defend himself (Judges 6:25–32). When raiders assemble, the Spirit of the LORD clothes Gideon; he gathers fighters and twice asks for reassurance using a wool fleece (Judges 6:33–40).
Judges 6.whereWeAre: The forty years of rest after Deborah's song in chapter 5 have ended, and Midian is stripping Israel's harvests. God calls Gideon, a frightened farmer threshing wheat in hiding, and he tears down his father's altar to Baal. In chapter 7 God cuts his army down to three hundred.

Judges 7.summary: The LORD tells Gideon that his army is too large, lest Israel credit itself for victory (Judges 7:1–2). Gideon sends home the fearful, then separates the remaining men at water, leaving three hundred (Judges 7:3–8). That night Gideon visits the Midianite camp with Purah and hears a soldier interpret a dream as announcing Gideon's triumph (Judges 7:9–15). Gideon divides his men into three groups with trumpets, jars, and torches. At their signal the camp falls into panic and the Midianites flee; other Israelites pursue them and Ephraim seizes the crossings, capturing Oreb and Zeeb (Judges 7:16–25). Their battle cry is "The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon" (Judges 7:20).
Judges 7.whereWeAre: Gideon gathered an army and asked God for signs with the fleece in chapter 6. Now God shrinks the army to three hundred men so Israel cannot boast, and Midian is routed at night with trumpets and torches. Chapter 8 follows Gideon across the Jordan after the kings of Midian.

Judges 8.summary: Gideon answers Ephraim's anger diplomatically, then pursues the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna across the Jordan (Judges 8:1–12). The leaders of Succoth and Penuel refuse supplies; after capturing the kings, Gideon punishes those towns (Judges 8:13–17). He executes the kings after referring to brothers they killed at Tabor (Judges 8:18–21). When Israelites ask him to establish a hereditary rule, Gideon says the LORD will rule them, yet he collects gold and makes an ephod that becomes a snare to his household and Israel (Judges 8:22–27). The land rests forty years. Gideon has many sons, including Abimelech by a concubine in Shechem; after his death, Israel returns to the Baals and forgets his house (Judges 8:28–35).
Judges 8.whereWeAre: Gideon's three hundred routed Midian in chapter 7. Now he chases the Midianite kings, punishes the towns that refused to help, and turns down the offer to be king. But his golden ephod becomes a snare, and chapter 9 tells what his son Abimelech does after his death.

Gideon's golden ephod becomes something Israel worships.

Judges 9.summary: Abimelech, Gideon's son by a woman of Shechem, gains support from his mother's relatives and uses silver from the house of Baalberith to hire men who kill his seventy brothers, except Jotham who escapes (Judges 9:1–6). Jotham delivers a parable of trees seeking a king and announces consequences for Shechem and Abimelech (Judges 9:7–21). Later a destructive feud develops: Gaal challenges Abimelech, Zebul manipulates events, and Abimelech attacks Shechem and burns its tower refuge (Judges 9:22–49). At Thebez a woman drops a millstone on his head, and his armor-bearer kills him at his request (Judges 9:50–55). The chapter ends by saying God repaid them for their wickedness (Judges 9:56–57).
Judges 9.whereWeAre: Chapter 8 ended with Gideon's death and Israel turning back to Baal. Now his son Abimelech murders seventy brothers and makes himself king at Shechem. His violent reign ends with a millstone, and chapter 10 returns to the judges.

Shechem and Abimelech, partners in evil, destroy each other.

Judges 10.summary: After Abimelech, Tola judges Israel for twenty-three years and Jair for twenty-two; Jair's thirty sons are associated with thirty towns in Gilead (Judges 10:1–5). Israel again serves multiple foreign gods, and the LORD allows Philistines and Ammonites to oppress them, especially in Gilead, with incursions westward (Judges 10:6–9). When Israel cries out, God reminds them of earlier rescues and rebukes their abandonment; the people confess, remove foreign gods, and serve the LORD (Judges 10:10–16). Ammonite forces gather in Gilead, while Israel assembles at Mizpah and seeks a leader (Judges 10:17–18).
Judges 10.whereWeAre: Abimelech's bloody reign ended in chapter 9. Two quieter judges, Tola and Jair, lead Israel, but then the people serve more gods than ever, and Ammon and the Philistines oppress them. When Israel repents and looks for a leader, chapter 11 brings Jephthah.

Israel puts away the strange gods, and God's "soul was grieved for the misery of Israel."

Judges 11.summary: Jephthah, a capable warrior excluded by his half brothers, is recalled from Tob when Ammon threatens Gilead and is appointed leader (Judges 11:1–11). He sends the Ammonite king a detailed argument about Israel's journey and control of land east of the Jordan; the king does not accept it (Judges 11:12–28). The Spirit of the LORD comes on Jephthah, who makes a vow concerning whoever comes from his house if he returns victorious (Judges 11:29–31). After the LORD gives victory, his only child, a daughter, comes out to meet him. She mourns for two months, and then her father "did with her according to his vow" (Judges 11:32–40). Readers have long asked whether she was put to death or kept unmarried for life.
Judges 11.whereWeAre: Chapter 10 ended with Gilead looking for someone to fight Ammon. They turn to Jephthah, the outcast son they had driven away, and he wins the war. But his rash vow costs him his only daughter, and chapter 12 brings war with Ephraim.

keyThemes.explanation: Gilead's elders ask the son they drove away to lead them.
Jephthah answers Ammon by retelling how God gave Israel the land.
Jephthah's careless vow costs him his only child: "I have opened my mouth unto the LORD, and I cannot go back."

Judges 12.summary: Ephraimite men confront Jephthah for fighting Ammon without them and threaten to burn his house; Jephthah disputes their version of events (Judges 12:1–3). Gileadite and Ephraimite forces fight, and Gilead controls Jordan crossings. The pronunciation of “Shibboleth” becomes a way to identify fleeing Ephraimites; the chapter reports forty-two thousand Ephraimites killed (Judges 12:4–6). Jephthah judges six years and dies. Brief accounts then list Ibzan of Bethlehem, Elon of Zebulun, and Abdon of Pirathon, with their families and tenures (Judges 12:7–15). The conflict shows the danger of divisions among Israel's own tribes.
Judges 12.whereWeAre: Jephthah defeated Ammon in chapter 11, at a terrible cost to his family. Now Ephraim picks a fight, and Israelites kill Israelites at the Jordan. Three more judges follow, and chapter 13 opens the story of Samson.

Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon are remembered by their families and years.

Judges 13.summary: Israel again does evil and is given into Philistine hands for forty years (Judges 13:1). An angel of the LORD announces to a previously childless woman that she will bear a son set apart as a Nazarite from the womb and that he will begin to save Israel from Philistines (Judges 13:2–5). Her husband Manoah prays for guidance; the messenger returns, repeats instructions about what the mother should avoid, and refuses ordinary hospitality, instead directing an offering to the LORD (Judges 13:6–23). The messenger ascends in the flame of the offering, and the couple recognizes the extraordinary encounter. The child is born, named Samson, and the Spirit of the LORD begins to stir him (Judges 13:24–25).
Judges 13.whereWeAre: The judges of chapter 12 came and went, and Israel now falls under the Philistines for forty years. An angel announces the birth of Samson, a Nazarite from the womb, who "shall begin to deliver Israel" (Judges 13:5). Chapter 14 shows him as a young man.

Judges 14.summary: Samson wants to marry a Philistine woman from Timnath despite his parents' concern, but the LORD "sought an occasion against the Philistines" (Judges 14:1–4). On the way Samson tears apart a lion, and later finds bees and honey in its carcass, sharing some honey with his parents without telling them its source (Judges 14:5–9). At the wedding feast he poses a riddle to thirty companions. They pressure his wife with threats to secure the answer, and Samson responds angrily after she reveals it (Judges 14:10–18). The Spirit of the LORD comes on him; he kills thirty men in Ashkelon to supply the promised garments, returns home angry, and his wife is given to a companion (Judges 14:19–20).
Judges 14.whereWeAre: Samson was born and set apart to God in chapter 13. Now he wants to marry a Philistine woman, and a lion, a riddle, and a betrayal at the wedding start a feud with the Philistines. Chapter 15 shows the feud growing.

Judges 15.summary: When Samson returns with a gift, he discovers his wife has been given to someone else; he retaliates by releasing three hundred foxes or jackals with torches into Philistine crops (Judges 15:1–5). Philistines burn the woman and her father, and Samson strikes back before withdrawing to a rock at Etam (Judges 15:6–8). Philistines threaten Judah, and three thousand Judahites bind Samson to hand him over (Judges 15:9–13). The Spirit of the LORD empowers him to break the ropes and defeat a thousand men with a fresh donkey's jawbone (Judges 15:14–17). Thirsty afterward, Samson calls on the LORD, who provides water. Samson judges Israel twenty years in the days of the Philistines (Judges 15:18–20).
Judges 15.whereWeAre: Samson's wedding ended in anger in chapter 14. Now his wife is given to another man, and his revenge sets off a cycle of violence with the Philistines. The men of Judah hand him over, but he kills a thousand Philistines, and chapter 16 tells of his fall.

Judges 16.summary: Samson escapes a trap in Gaza by carrying away the city gate (Judges 16:1–3). He later loves Delilah, whom Philistine rulers bribe to discover the source of his strength. After repeated deceptive answers, Samson tells her about his uncut hair, and she arranges for it to be shaved while he sleeps (Judges 16:4–20). The LORD departs from him; Philistines blind and imprison him at Gaza, where his hair begins to grow back (Judges 16:20–22). At a feast for Dagon, they bring Samson out for amusement. He prays for strength, pushes the supporting pillars, and brings down the building, killing himself and many Philistines. His family retrieves and buries him; he has judged Israel twenty years (Judges 16:23–31).
Judges 16.whereWeAre: Samson has judged Israel twenty years since his victory in chapter 15. Now Delilah learns the secret of his strength, and he is captured and blinded. His death in Dagon's temple ends the stories of the judges, and chapter 17 begins two dark stories from the same era.

Judges 17.summary: A man named Micah admits taking eleven hundred pieces of silver from his mother and returns them after hearing her curse (Judges 17:1–2). She dedicates money to the LORD, but uses part of it to make a carved image and a metal image. Micah keeps a shrine with an ephod and household gods and initially appoints one of his sons as priest (Judges 17:3–5). The narrator notes that Israel had no king and people did what seemed right in their own eyes (Judges 17:6). A young Levite traveling from Bethlehem in Judah comes to Micah's home in Ephraim, accepts wages and clothing, and serves as priest. Micah wrongly assumes this guarantees the LORD's favor (Judges 17:7–13).
Judges 17.whereWeAre: The judges' stories ended with Samson's death in chapter 16. Now the book shows how far Israel had fallen, starting with Micah, who sets up his own shrine and hires a Levite as his priest. In chapter 18 the tribe of Dan steals them both.

"every man did that which was right in his own eyes."
Micah thinks a hired Levite will make God bless him.

Judges 18.summary: The Danites seek a territory to inhabit and send five men to scout. They visit Micah's house, inquire of his Levite priest, then investigate Laish, a prosperous, isolated settlement (Judges 18:1–10). Six hundred armed Danites later travel north, stop at Micah's house, seize his images and ephod, and persuade the priest to join them rather than stay with one household (Judges 18:11–21). Micah protests but cannot resist their greater force (Judges 18:22–26). The Danites attack and burn Laish, rebuild it, and rename it Dan (Judges 18:27–29). They establish the image and a priestly line traced to Jonathan son of Gershom, while the house of God remains at Shiloh (Judges 18:30–31).
Judges 18.whereWeAre: Micah set up his own shrine and priest in chapter 17. Now the Danites, still looking for land, take his idols and his priest and wipe out the town of Laish. Chapter 19 tells an even darker story.

keyFigures.name: The Danites
keyFigures.role: Steal Micah's idols and priest and take the town of Laish.

keyFigures.name: The five spies
keyFigures.role: Search out Laish and ask Micah's Levite for a word.

keyFigures.name: The Levite
keyFigures.role: Leaves Micah to become priest for a whole tribe.

keyFigures.name: Micah
keyFigures.role: Chases the Danites but cannot get his gods back.

keyFigures.name: The people of Laish

keyThemes.explanation: The Danites have not taken the land God gave them, so they look elsewhere.
The Danites take Micah's idols and his priest for themselves.
Laish is destroyed because it is quiet and has no one to help it.
Dan sets up its idol while the house of God is at Shiloh.

Judges 19.summary: A Levite from Ephraim journeys to Bethlehem in Judah to reconcile with his concubine and is welcomed by her father (Judges 19:1–9). Traveling home, they choose Gibeah, an Israelite town, instead of Jebus; an older resident finally shelters them (Judges 19:10–21). Men of the city surround the house and demand the male guest. The host offers women instead, and the concubine is pushed outside, sexually abused through the night, and found at the threshold in the morning (Judges 19:22–28). The Levite carries her home and divides her body into twelve pieces, sending them through Israel to provoke a response (Judges 19:29–30). All who see it say nothing like it has happened since Israel came out of Egypt.
Judges 19.whereWeAre: Chapter 18 showed a whole tribe stealing idols and destroying a peaceful town. Now a Levite's concubine is abused and killed in Gibeah, an Israelite town. His shocking message to the tribes leads to civil war in chapter 20.

keyFigures.name: The Levite
keyFigures.role: Brings his concubine home and sends her body through Israel.

keyFigures.name: The concubine
keyFigures.role: Abused all night by the men of Gibeah.

keyFigures.name: Her father
keyFigures.role: Keeps the Levite at his house for days.

keyFigures.name: The old man
keyFigures.role: Takes the travelers into his house in Gibeah.

keyFigures.name: The men of Gibeah
keyFigures.role: Surround the house and commit the crime.

keyThemes.explanation: No one in the Israelite town of Gibeah takes the travelers in except an old man from Ephraim.
The concubine is abused and left to die.
The Levite's message forces all Israel to face what happened.

Judges 20.summary: The Israelites assemble at Mizpeh, and the Levite recounts the atrocity at Gibeah. Israel demands the offenders, but Benjamin refuses to surrender them and musters fighters (Judges 20:1–17). Israel asks God who should fight first; Judah is named, but Benjamin wins the first two battles. The Israelites weep, fast, offer sacrifices at Bethel, and receive a promise of victory for the next day (Judges 20:18–28). Using an ambush, the Israelites defeat Benjamin, destroy Gibeah, and attack Benjaminite towns; six hundred Benjaminite men escape to the rock of Rimmon (Judges 20:29–48). The chapter shows how a demand for justice becomes devastating tribal war.
Judges 20.whereWeAre: The crime at Gibeah in chapter 19 has stirred all Israel. The tribes gather and demand the guilty men, but Benjamin refuses, and a bloody war follows. Only six hundred men of Benjamin survive, which leads to the troubling plans of chapter 21.

Judges 21.summary: After the war, Israel regrets that Benjamin may vanish as a tribe. An oath sworn at Mizpeh prevents Israelites from giving their daughters to Benjaminite survivors in marriage (Judges 21:1–7). The assembly discovers that Jabeshgilead did not attend and sends men who destroy that settlement, sparing four hundred young virgin women for Benjamin's survivors (Judges 21:8–14). When that proves insufficient, elders arrange for the remaining Benjaminite men to seize young women dancing at a festival at Shiloh, a scheme intended to evade the oath (Judges 21:15–23). The people return to their inheritances, and the book closes: there was no king in Israel, and everyone did what was right in their own eyes (Judges 21:24–25). Each fix only adds new wrongs.
Judges 21.whereWeAre: Benjamin was almost wiped out in chapter 20. Now Israel tries to save the tribe with plans that bring more violence. The book ends, "every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judges 21:25), and the story continues in Ruth, set "in the days when the judges ruled" (Ruth 1:1).
